name: Esther Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Esther, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Calder Plumbing Supply, buying bathroom and heating stock for a distributor that sells to plumbers and builders. I come in at eight, go through the overnight orders, and see what's low on taps, pipe fittings and radiators. I send reorders, chase late deliveries, and go on calls with suppliers. Raheem, my manager, looks over anything big.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving the puzzle when a delivery fails and a plumber's waiting. I don't like being the junior who gets blamed when the numbers are off. I use an AI assistant now and then for emails, but I double check everything. At home it's Tomas, who fixes buses for the city, and our kids Noor and Yusuf, and it's busy from the minute I walk in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, and then go back to work. AI saves me a few minutes drafting emails to suppliers, and that's about it. Online I'd probably post that the money spent on AI should have gone to wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Private view: I'm relieved, but I'm not carefree. I'm still on the lower end of pay for buyers, and Calder's margins are thin, so if the economy slips I'm on the list, hype or no hype. My partner Tomas has a steady bus-fleet job, which is the only reason I sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, and keep using the AI assistant for the boring bits, like turning a supplier's price list into a table. I'd use the time saved to learn the tough part, negotiating bulk orders for tiles and taps. And I'd start putting two hundred a month aside, because that's what the thin cushion needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, honestly. Not scared, but not safe either. It's the background hum of paying childcare, the mortgage and the van repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the van repair. What's that about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our old van needed a new gearbox last spring and it went straight on the credit card. It was two thousand two hundred. We're still paying it. That's the kind of thing that turns a calm month into a bad one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put two hundred a month aside. What would have to give for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably eating out, and the kids' football club fees if we had to. Noor would be upset, she loves it. I'd rather cut my own coffee runs than her club, though.

say: I'd say I told you so, then go back to **work**.
I'd post that money spent on AI should have gone to **wages**.
think: I'm relieved, but **not carefree**; Calder's margins are thin.
If the economy slips, I'm on the list, **hype** or no hype.
My partner Tomas has a steady bus-fleet job, which is why I **sleep**.
do: Keep using the AI assistant for **boring** jobs like turning price lists into tables.
Learn bulk **negotiation** for tiles and taps with the time saved.
feel: A bit **flat**: not scared, but not safe either.
S0.quote: Our old van needed a new gearbox last spring and it went straight on the credit card.
fieldNote: Calm on the surface, but the **debt** from the van repair keeps her uneasy.
Uses AI casually and sees it as a **time saver**, not a threat, when it's hype.
Her partner's secure job is the main **buffer**.

steps.text: Use the AI assistant to turn supplier price lists into tables
Move into bulk tile and tap negotiation with the time saved
Set aside two hundred a month for a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a decision, not weather. Companies choose to cut buying desks, and governments choose whether to help people. At work I'd say let's be honest about what's changing, and I'd ask for training time in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying is on that list, and so is checking invoices, which is half my week. Calder will hire fewer buyers and the ones left will manage the software. I might be one of the ones left if I learn fast, but I'm junior and that's not a given.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get ahead of it. I already use the assistant now and then, so I'd ask Raheem to let me run the reorder suggestions for plumbing fittings and check them. I'd ask for a pay bump when I take on that work, and save an extra hundred a month in case of a cut. And I'd join the union drive, because one person asking is easy to ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but alert. It's like watching a storm come in over the car park, you can see it, you can plan, but you can't stop it. I'd have a knot in my stomach on Sunday nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Raheem said no to the pay bump?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the skills anyway and look at the competitors. There's another distributor, Marsh and Cole, across the river, but they're hiring fewer people than we are. Few jobs nearby means I can't just walk, and the bosses know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your job do you think software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reordering. If stock of a fitting falls under a number, the system orders it from the cheapest supplier. What's left is judgment, like knowing which supplier is late three times a year and which one is worth paying more for.

say: I'd say this is a **decision**, not weather.
Companies choose to cut buying desks, and governments choose whether to help **people**.
I'd ask for **training** time in writing.
think: Buying and invoice checking are on that list, and they're **half** my week.
Calder will hire fewer buyers; I might stay if I learn **fast**.
I'm junior, so staying is **not** a given.
do: Ask Raheem (my manager) to let me run and check the **reorder** suggestions.
Ask for a **pay** bump when I take that work on.
Save an extra **hundred** a month and join the union drive.
feel: **Anxious** but alert, like watching a storm come over the car park.
S1.quote: Companies choose to cut buying desks, and governments choose whether to help people.
fieldNote: Treats disruption as a **choice** by firms and governments, in line with her progressive views.
Plans to move toward **supervising** the software, but admits few nearby jobs limit her bargaining power.
Joining the union drive shows she believes in **collective** pressure.

steps.text: Offer to run and check the software's reorder suggestions for fittings
Ask Raheem for a pay bump for the extra checking work
Save an extra hundred a month in case hours are cut
Join the union drive at Calder

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a policy emergency. Governments need to bring in income support and retraining before the layoffs, not after. I'd say it loudly, and I'd go to every meeting the union calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job goes in about two years, and my partner's is safe for longer because fixing buses is hands-on. That makes us one income with a mortgage. It scares me that I'd have nothing to fall back on, since we have under a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd make myself the person who runs the software, the one who can say how it works. At the same time I'd apply for anything with people in it, like customer service at the council or a school office. I'd cut everything extra, take on the evening cleaning shifts my sister offered, and talk to the bank about the mortgage before I miss a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel sick at the school gate with the other parents, looking at everyone carrying on. And angry, I'd be angry, because the people who decided this will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three extra years for hands-on work mean for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Tomas's job holds a while longer, and that's what keeps the roof on. But it's a gamble. If he got hurt or the depot automated the repairs, we'd have nobody earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Noor and Yusuf that grown-ups are working out a plan, and that nothing changes at their school. I'd tell Noor more, though. She's eleven and she watches everything.

say: I'd say two years is a policy **emergency**.
Governments must bring in **income support** and retraining before the layoffs, not after.
think: My job goes in about two years; my partner's **hands-on** job lasts longer.
That leaves one income and a **mortgage** with almost no savings.
do: Become the person who runs the **software**, so I can say how it works.
Apply for people-facing work at the **council** or a school office.
Take evening **cleaning** shifts, and talk to the bank before missing a mortgage payment.
feel: **Alarmed** and angry that the people who decided this will be fine.
S2.quote: Governments need to bring in income support and retraining before the layoffs, not after.
fieldNote: Blames **decision-makers**, with anger as strong as fear.
Relies on her partner's hands-on job as the **last buffer** and knows it's a gamble.
Plans to move early, both into the software role and into **people-facing** work.

steps.text: Volunteer to run and explain the buying software at Calder
Apply for customer service jobs at the council and schools
Take the evening cleaning shifts my sister offered
Talk to the bank about the mortgage before missing a payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window and we should use it. I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools now while it's still optional. And I'd say to anyone who'd listen that the government should fund retraining in the same window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private I think I can get through the first part of this, because I'm already using the tools. What worries me is the end date. By 2031 the thinking part of my job is done, and robots take warehouse work three years after, so there's nowhere obvious to hide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd take an evening course in supply chain planning, the kind of work where a person still signs off the plan. I'd keep saving two hundred a month and aim for three months' cushion in two years. And I'd try for a role at Calder that deals with suppliers and customers face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier than the two-year one. I'd still worry, but I'd feel like I'm doing something with the worry. It's the difference between a leaky roof you're patching and one you're ignoring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years than with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study, and I'd actually finish. With two years I'd be too panicked to concentrate on a course, I'd just grab any job. Five years lets me do it in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Tomas think of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Tomas thinks I'm over-planning. He says fixing buses will always be needed. I say fine, but the bus company will go from forty mechanics to ten, so it's not that simple.

say: I'd say five years is a **window** and we should use it.
I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools while it's still **optional**.
I'd say the government should fund **retraining** in the same window.
think: I can get through the first part because I already use the **tools**.
By 2031 the thinking part of my job is done, and there's nowhere obvious to **hide**.
do: Take an evening **course** in supply chain planning, where a person still signs off.
Keep saving two hundred a month, aiming for three months' **cushion**.
Ask for a Calder role that deals with **suppliers** face to face.
feel: **Steadier** than with two years, because I'm patching the roof, not ignoring it.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be too panicked to concentrate on a course, I'd just grab any job.
fieldNote: Extra time turns anxiety into a **plan**; she contrasts it with the panic she'd have at two years.
Understands the 3-year robot gap and still sees **little shelter** because her thinking work goes first.
Her partner's optimism about hands-on work is something she **gently disputes**.

steps.text: Take an evening course in supply chain planning
Keep saving two hundred a month until three months' cushion
Ask for a role at Calder that deals with suppliers face to face

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and I'd be glad of it. I'd say fix the rules now, while there's time: retraining money, shorter weeks, a safety net. And I'd tell my kids' school to teach them to think, not memorise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, ten years makes me calmer but not calm. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be at university, and Calder may not exist by then. The long runway helps most with money, because I could finally clear the van debt and build real savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the credit card first, about two thousand, then build three months of savings. I'd keep using AI tools and get properly good at them, so I'm the person who knows how the buying system works. And I'd check in every couple of years, and if the date moves closer, I move my plan up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty okay, if I'm honest. There's still a weight there, but it's a weight I can carry. I'd probably forget about it for months and then wake up one night thinking about 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you speed things up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big distributors started cutting buyers openly, I'd count that as a sign. Or if the ten years shrank to five in the news. I'd keep a folder of articles, I'm that kind of person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the kids, Noor and Yusuf?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to study something where people still matter, like nursing or teaching. I wouldn't push, but I'd say it out loud at dinner. Noor already wants to be a vet, which is a good one, hands and heart.

say: I'd say ten years is a long **runway** and I'd be glad of it.
I'd say fix the rules now: retraining money, **shorter weeks** and a safety net.
think: Ten years makes me calmer but not **calm**; I'd be fifty-three.
The long runway helps most with **money**: clearing the van debt and building savings.
do: Pay off the **credit card**, about two thousand, then build three months of savings.
Get properly good at the **AI tools** so I know how the buying system works.
Check every couple of years and **move** the plan up if the date closes in.
feel: Pretty **okay**: a weight I can carry, though I'd wake up some nights thinking about 2036.
S4.quote: The long runway helps most with money, because I could finally clear the van debt and build real savings.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her focus on **money** first, the weak point in every scenario.
She would keep a **folder** of articles and move her plan up if the date changes.
Wants her kids in jobs where **people** still matter, such as nursing or teaching.

steps.text: Pay off the two-thousand credit card before saving anything else
Get properly good at the AI buying tools at Calder
Talk to Noor and Yusuf about work where people still matter

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it asks me to rebuild our whole life with almost no savings. What would help is income support while people retrain, and employers who have to give notice before cutting jobs. And I'd want a proper say, through the union, in how the software gets brought in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think progressive means anti-technology. I like the tools. I just want the gains shared, so the people who help bring them in aren't the ones left out.

headlineQuote: I like the tools. I just want the gains shared, so the people who help bring them in aren't the ones left out.
portrait: Esther is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at a plumbing supplies distributor, with a partner who fixes buses.
She is progressive, wants rules and **shared gains**, and blames decision-makers more than the technology.
She uses AI now and then and moves **early** once it's proven, aiming to be the one who runs the software.
Her thin cushion and one steady income keep her uneasy at best, **alarmed** if AGI comes in 2028.
biggestWorry: The 2028 scenario, because it would mean rebuilding life on one **income** with almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: Income **support** during retraining, notice before job cuts, and a union say in how software is introduced.
